Run 3 surrogate diagnostics

Run 3 contains the intended 100 nominal designs and 400 single-mirror perturbations. This change improves prediction magnitudes on the initial validation designs, but the model still learns the wrong local responses at many points selected by PSO. Feedback mostly corrects nominal power while leaving perturbation sensitivity inaccurate. Run 3 also found a substantially better Finesse design early in the search, then repeatedly selected worse ones.

These results use saved Finesse labels, saved production checkpoints, and the original captured PSO evaluations. The new fitting experiments write separate diagnostic checkpoints. No production training, checkpoint, data file, or optical power simulation was changed.

What was checked

The diagnostic loader now reads the initial HDF5 design_group_size attribute. Run 3 therefore has 100 five-row initial groups, while historical run 2 retains 100 two-row nominal/joint groups. Five-row direction ordering is checked for both initial and feedback data. Treating run 3 as consecutive pairs would have silently produced incorrect nominal/partner associations.

The full run 3 audit contains 140 groups and 700 rows: 500 initial rows and 200 feedback rows. Of the initial groups, 78 have valid fixed q throughout; 22 do not. Initial data contains 104 zero-power rows and 230 rows in the saved 282.09 +/- 0.01 W center band. Production training includes these rows; valid-q subsets below are explicitly identified. Zero labels do not establish whether a cavity was unstable or a solver/lock failed.

All 25 feature reconstructions from feedback rounds 1, 10, 20, 30, and 40 passed the documented tolerances. This supports the sampled feature path; it does not validate optical power solves. Artifacts: full audit, feature audit.

The initial sampling change helped, but did not fix response signs

The two runs share identical nominal features and identical initial training and validation design IDs. Both base checkpoints were evaluated on the same 15 valid held-out run 3 designs, containing 75 rows and 60 directional responses. This avoids comparing different response types or different geometries.

Base checkpoint Power MAE (W) DeltaPower MAE (W) Perturbation-cost MAE (W/m) Correct significant signs
Run 2 8.123 1.213 0.478 2/10
Run 3 7.124 0.642 0.235 2/10

Run 3 reduces difference error by about 47% and perturbation-cost error by about 51% on this cohort. The sample count and significance threshold matter: only 10 of these 60 responses have absolute true differences above 0.1 W.

The response shape is still wrong. Across all 78 valid initial designs, Finesse power decreases in both ITM directions for 59 designs and in both ETM directions for 62 designs. The run 3 base model predicts opposite signs for the two directions in every one of the 78 designs, for both mirrors. On the held-out subset, Finesse has 11/15 ITM and 13/15 ETM pairs with both directions decreasing; the model has zero such pairs.

Most initial responses are small: only 52 of 312 valid directional labels exceed 0.1 W. Typical signed changes are a few thousandths of a watt. The ROC steps average about 0.012-0.013 input standard deviations. Matching the sampling pattern therefore does not by itself force accurate local slopes and curvature. See training audit.

Accuracy where run 3 actually searches

The following checkpoints were evaluated on exactly the same 40 run 3 feedback designs. The final run 3 checkpoint has already trained on these feedback labels, so its result measures replay reconstruction.

Checkpoint DeltaPower MAE (W) Correct significant signs
Run 2 base 10.250 2/131
Run 3 base 10.001 2/131
Run 3 after round 40 9.935 48/131

Both run 3 base and final checkpoints get every significant ETM response wrong: 0/67 correct. The final checkpoint improves nominal powers and some ITM signs, but differences remain much too flat.

At round 40, the final checkpoint gives this concrete example:

Sample Finesse power (W) Final MLP power (W) Finesse DeltaPower (W) MLP DeltaPower (W)
Nominal 39.974 38.797 0 0
ITM+ 29.276 38.797 -10.698 approximately 0
ITM- 53.213 38.796 +13.239 approximately 0
ETM+ 62.251 38.586 +22.277 -0.211
ETM- 23.766 39.008 -16.208 +0.211

The true perturbation cost is 9.528 W/m; the final model predicts about 0.0500 W/m, roughly 190 times too small. The nominal power is quite close, yet the sensitivity driving the optimization objective is badly wrong.

Across all 40 feedback updates, evaluating the matching checkpoint immediately before and after its update gives nominal-power MAE 11.395 -> 7.151 W, while DeltaPower MAE stays essentially unchanged at 9.929 -> 9.937 W. Those reconstructed predictions use stored float32 features; original captured online records are kept separately, since tiny predicted differences can change sign under feature rounding.

Artifacts: checkpoint comparison, feedback updates.

The actual PSO outcome is mixed

Costs use the saved full objective:

0.5 / nominal_power + 0.5 * sum(abs(DeltaPower) / ROC_step).

Run 3's best saved Finesse cost was approximately 0.01694 at round 4, compared with 0.59014 for run 2's best saved design. Lower is better: run 3 found a design about 35 times better under this objective.

Later it repeatedly chose poor designs that the surrogate scored as nearly flat. At round 40, the original online prediction was cost 0.0380 versus Finesse cost 4.7766, about 126 times larger. The original round-40 evaluation used checkpoint 39; this is distinct from the final-checkpoint replay above. The saved records retain every earlier good design, so the final round alone does not describe the best result achieved by the run.

Online mean true cost was 0.975 for run 2 and 2.996 for run 3. This describes each run's own selected trajectory; it is not a controlled same-point model comparison. All captured costs were reconstructed from their original powers, steps, and weights and checked against the saved values.

Directly supervising differences helps local fitting

Separate models fitted the 25 saved rows from rounds 1, 10, 20, 30, and 40 for up to 2,000 epochs. Within each experiment, loss variants shared identical initial weights, normalization, and training settings (one seed, 9302). Checkpoints were selected using the same training power/difference score.

Initialization and scaling Current row loss: DeltaPower MAE (W) Paired loss: DeltaPower MAE (W)
Fresh weights, scaling from these 25 rows 3.276 0.290
Production final checkpoint, original scaling 4.945 1.603

The paired objective adds an explicit signed-difference penalty. It improves these fits by about 91% and 68%, respectively. The center-focused and ordinary log-power variants give identical results here because the selected labels lie outside the narrow center band. Most selected checkpoints reach the epoch budget, so the residual errors do not establish a model capacity limit.

Local fitting does not establish a usable global surrogate. The fresh models were also evaluated on the other 35 feedback groups without further training. Both produced extreme powers at the distant round-4 design, whose ITM ROC is at the opposite end of the global range from the five training designs. The ordinary and paired maximum difference errors reached roughly 6.6e161 W and 1.4e136 W. Their median difference errors were 0.628 W and 0.284 W, but the extreme failures dominate their mean errors. Small-set normalization and coverage make these checkpoints unsuitable for global PSO use.

Artifacts: fresh fits, final-checkpoint fits, ordinary transfer evaluation, paired transfer evaluation.

Interpretation and next experiment

The change to four-direction initial sampling was useful. The remaining failure is that row-wise log-power training and checkpoint selection do not directly require the differences consumed by PSO to be correct. The observed flat feedback predictions, wrong symmetric response shape, and improvement under paired supervision support investigating this training objective. They do not isolate loss, scaling, coverage, optimization budget, and feedback selection as independent causes. With 400 rather than 160 initial training rows, the same batch size gives 13 rather than 5 optimizer updates per epoch. The automatic newest-feedback weight also changes from 40 to 100. The run comparison therefore measures the actual combined intervention, rather than an isolated sampling-layout effect.

A controlled next experiment should keep the full initial design split, global training-only scaling, model initialization, batching, and budget fixed; compare current and paired supervision; select checkpoints using validation power and signed-difference errors; and then assess held-out designs and actual Finesse-verified optimization results. Dense response or independent-q sampling could address coverage separately. The best Finesse-verified design should also be tracked alongside the latest round.

No global retraining comparison or production change was made here.
